extracted.intended_audience: writers, playwrights, opera directors, critics, and genteel readers
extracted.subtask_short: writing polite essays and theatre criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative principles for composing polite-society essays and for critiquing/staging theatrical entertainments (especially opera), with emphasis on style, moral purpose, and theatrical plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discourse for female audiences: refine, do not debase
rubrics_metrics.description: "Discourse for their Entertainment, is not to be debased but refined." When addressing women (e.g. 'Tea-Table Talk'), use a style and manner suited to their understanding: exalt the subjects rather than lower them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing pieces intended for female readers, adopt a 'Stile and Air' appropriate to their understanding: elevate topics, avoid coarseness, and aim to furnish agreeable, improving conversation. The author also promises discretion about lovers' private glances but will expose false protestations in public assemblies — i.e., balance tact with moral candour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mix shadows and realities in a theatrical piece
rubrics_metrics.description: "Shadows and Realities ought not to be mix'd together in the same Piece; and that Scenes, which are designed as the Representations of Nature, should be filled with Resemblances, and not with the Things themselves."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage representations of nature should rely on theatrical resemblances (painted scenes, implied action) rather than inserting literal items that break the representational logic (e.g., painted countryside plus real live sheep). Mixing real objects with theatrical illusions invites ridicule and breaks the audience's willing suspension of disbelief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid childish or absurd machines and decorations
rubrics_metrics.description: "There should be nothing in the Scenes and Machines which may appear Childish and Absurd."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extravagant decoration is permissible when its purpose is to gratify the senses, but designers must avoid elements that look ridiculous (example: a tempest shown by an actor in ermine sailing on a pasteboard sea, dragons spitting wild-fire, or incongruous real cascades). Keep spectacle within bounds of common sense and good workmanship to avoid inviting mockery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use resemblances rather than real items when representing nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenes designed as representations of nature should be filled with resemblances, and not with the things themselves (e.g., represent herds by painted scenes, not by crowding the stage with live animals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical theatrical representation favors suggestive devices over literal inclusion. Examples show that placing real animals or objects on stage (sheep, oxen) for a painted landscape is an inconsistency and an aesthetic fault; prefer theatrical signs that evoke rather than attempt literal reproduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about using live animals or improbable real elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Anecdotes of sparrows used in an opera and of a proposed invasion of mice (Whittington story) illustrate that live animals onstage may mislead the audience, produce practical inconveniences, or create absurd situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Live animals can distract, cause mishaps, infest the theatre, or produce implausible effects (e.g., birds flying but music supplied from offstage). Consider safety, practicality, and the risk of undermining the piece's dignity before employing real creatures; false shows (offstage music) are also deceptive to audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure spectacle fits the genre's purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: "An Opera may be allowed to be extravagantly lavish in its Decorations, as its only Design is to gratify the Senses," but even so, common sense requires avoiding childishness and absurdity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the level and type of spectacle to the work's intent: operas may emphasize sensory display, while other genres demand different balances. Even in spectacle-driven works, retain internal coherence and avoid elements that contradict the audience's expectations for the genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor concise, classical diction over florid circumlocution
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of modern Italian writers: they use 'such a florid form of Words, and such tedious Circumlocutions ... and at the same time, fill their Writings with such poor Imaginations and Conceits.' One good line of Virgil is valued above all the 'Clincant' or tinsel of Tasso.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer clear, elevated, and substantive expression (classical exemplars like Virgil) to ornate but empty verbal ornament. Avoid pedantic verbosity and cheap conceits that impress by glitter rather than by genuine poetic worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply learning and wit to virtuous ends; do not polish understanding at the expense of manners
rubrics_metrics.description: "To polish our Understandings and neglect our Manners is of all things the most inexcusable." The essay argues that wit and learning are defects, not merits, if disconnected from good conduct; the 'whole man is to move together' and actions should have a prospect of public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating writers, speakers, or public figures, value the ethical application of talent. Wit that flatters vice or that exists for mere display (how rather than what) is blameworthy. Assess works and authors for both intellectual polish and moral purpose — modesty and integrity are chief ornaments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess the social tendency of an author's work: relation to reason, religion, and good breeding
rubrics_metrics.description: The general tendency of our indifferent actions (and by extension our public writings and behaviour) ought to be agreeable to the Dictates of Reason, of Religion, of good Breeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should look beyond cleverness to the societal effects of a piece: does it encourage virtuous habits or merely fashionable affectations? Politeness and vogue are insufficient; works should be judged by whether they incline readers toward reason, piety, and proper conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate silent observation as a source of penetrating judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The author claims a 'Resignation of Speech' gives him advantages as an observer: 'I have ... a more than ordinary Penetration in Seeing ... and make shrewd Guesses ... at the inmost Thoughts and Reflections of all whom I behold.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers and critics should value careful, silent observation of manners and countenances as material for writing. Refrain from needless speech; let attentive perception inform characterizations and moral judgments in essays and criticisms.
